text:
SASRec perturbations mix several mechanisms: deleting an interaction removes evidence, changes causal attention context, and—after compaction and left-repadding—may shift surviving items’ learned positional embeddings. Removing the latest item also changes the final query item. The [original implementation](https://github.com/kang205/SASRec/blob/master/model.py) adds absolute position embeddings and scores from the final sequence position, so recent-versus-old deletion effects alone cannot establish temporal reliance. [Revisiting SASRec](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.09596v1) additionally raises padding and positional-alignment concerns, although its proposed corrections are hypotheses rather than demonstrated explanations.

Suggested controls, inferred from these architectural mechanisms: compare equal-sized recent, older, and random removals within the same users; stratify by history length and match removed-item frequency. Compare ordinary deletion/repacking with position-preserving removal using explicit attention masks and unchanged surviving position IDs; zeroing embeddings alone may leave positional or attention effects. Separate last-item removal from recent-window removal that retains the last item. Use local shuffling with the same item multiset, occupied positions, and final item to probe order sensitivity without removing evidence; shuffling still changes causal context, so it does not isolate transition reliance perfectly.

Keep candidate IDs and the original seen-item exclusion mask fixed across perturbations: deleted history items must not become newly eligible recommendations. Report paired score-margin changes alongside rank changes, uncertainty, and per-category results. Interpret these as model sensitivity under specified interventions, not causal evidence about user preferences. [CETD](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/20/11176) reinforces the need to preserve temporal dependencies and plausible histories when constructing counterfactual explanations.
